props.title: Nestor, the Long-Eared Christmas Donkey
props.initialSlug: A brave donkey helps guide Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem

sections.content: Rankin/Bass Productions, the stop-motion animation pioneers behind Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer (1964) and Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town (1970), created this darker, more emotionally complex Christmas special. Nestor, the Long-Eared Christmas Donkey (1977) adapts the Biblical nativity story through the lens of a misfit animal tale, much like their earlier success with Rudolph. The special stands out for tackling heavier themes - death of a parent, persecution, and faith - while maintaining the signature Animagic puppet animation style.

sections.content: The special follows the template established by The Little Drummer Boy (1968), another Rankin/Bass Biblical adaptation that centers on a character who aids Mary and Joseph's journey to Bethlehem. Roger Miller's narration as Speiltoe the dog mirrors Burl Ives' Sam the Snowman from Rudolph, providing both story context and musical interludes. The production demonstrates Rankin/Bass's willingness to explore more serious narrative territory in their later specials, similar to The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus (1985).

While less frequently aired than other Rankin/Bass classics, Nestor's story connects to a broader tradition of Christmas specials focused on outcast characters finding their purpose. This theme appears in The Most Wonderful Time of the Year (1974) and Frosty the Snowman (1969), though Nestor's tale carries more explicit religious overtones. The special's message about embracing differences rather than viewing them as flaws remains particularly relevant. SUBHEAD: Religious Themes in Animated Holiday Specials

sections.content: Nestor represents a unique intersection between secular holiday entertainment and religious storytelling. While most Christmas animation of the era focused on Santa Claus mythology, this special, along with The Little Drummer Boy (1968) and The First Christmas: The Story of the First Christmas Snow (1975), directly engaged with the nativity narrative. This approach influenced later religious-themed animation like The Small One (1978), Disney's short film about a donkey sold to carry Mary to Bethlehem.
